newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria Shell talks to Ogonis to restart work.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria Shell talks to Ogonis to restart work.

text.p: Royal Dutch Shell Group's Nigerian operation on Wednesday said it had begun talks in politically volatile Ogoniland which may lead to an eventual return to oil production.

Egbert Imomoh, General Manager of Shell's Eastern Division, said meetings had already been held with local chiefs and youth groups. "I will be meeting 30 other people on Thursday," he told reporters in the southern city of Port Harcourt.
"Our plan is to return to Ogoniland and clean up the pollution in the area, start community assistance projects, take stock of our facilities and when the time is right, start production again."
Shell pulled out Ogoniland in 1993 following the sabotage of installations and attacks on its staff by the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni People (MOSOP).

Shell has been harassed by campaigners for its activities in Nigeria since November, when military rulers ordered the execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other MOSOP minority rights activists for the murder of four pro-government chiefs.
MOSOP was campaigning for self-determination for the 500,000 Ogonis and compensation from Shell for damage its operations had caused to the local environment.
Shell's offer to talk to the Ogonis about cleaning up the region was made in May, but MOSOP rejected it out of hand as, "No more than a publicity exercise."
"We haven't met any MOSOP group or any group calling itself MOSOP. If they come we'll talk to them," Imomoh said.
Nineteen MOSOP supporters were detained in May 1995 for complicity in the same crimes as Saro-Wiwa.
Their lawyer claims that one of them has died as a result of conditions in Port Harcourt prison, but this has not been independently confirmed.
The current production potential of Ogoniland is estimated by Shell at 28,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude, down from a peak of 108,000 bpd in 1973.
Shell pumps about half Nigeria's nearly two million bpd of crude oil.
Acts of sabotage, not necessarily politically-motivated, remain a problem in southeastern Rivers state, one of the most densely populated oil-producing areas in the world.
Leaks at Shell pipelines in the state, where Ogoniland is located, forced the closure of pipelines and flow stations three times in July and August.
